bib.title: Larger language models do in-context learning differently

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Larger language models do in-context learning differently", Jerry Wei, Jason Wei, Yi Tay, Dustin Tran, Albert Webson, Yifeng Lu, Xinyun Chen, Hanxiao Liu, Da Huang, Denny Zhou, Tengyu Ma (Google Research, Brain Team; Stanford; Brown). arXiv:2303.03846v2, March 2023. Preprint.

COVERAGE: Extraction was clean. I read the main text (pp.1-9) and the appendices A, B.1-B.6, C.1, C.2 (start), C.3 (start), C.4 and the start of D. The 132,165-char text came from 51 pages. I skimmed the reference list and the Appendix D prompt dumps (dataset examples, one of which is offensive ETHOS text), and read none of the per-dataset figure data. Figures 16-21 are plots, so their numbers were not extracted.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Overriding semantic priors with flipped in-context labels is an emergent ability of scale.
 - number: text-davinci-002 averages 90.3% accuracy at 0% flipped labels and 22.5% at 100% flipped labels.
 - setup: Fig 2. Average over 6 binary tasks (SST-2, SUBJ, QQP, RTE, FP, ETHOS; TREC excluded because it has 6 classes). 100 eval examples per dataset, k=16 exemplars per class. Eval labels are not flipped, so a model that fully follows the flipped exemplars scores near 0%.
 - quote: "Large models, on the other hand, experience performance drops to well-below random guessing (e.g,. text-davinci-002 performance drops from 90.3% with 0% ﬂipped labels to just 22.5% with 100% ﬂipped labels)."
 - where: p.4, Section 3
2. Small models ignore flipped labels. All GPT-3 models (ada to davinci, 175B) count as "small".
 - number: none
 - setup: Fig 2, same as above. GPT-3, InstructGPT, Codex and PaLM (8B/62B/540B) were all tested.
 - quote: "Note that GPT-3 models can remove semantic priors (i.e., perform at guessing accuracy) but cannot override them (i.e., perform signiﬁcantly worse than guessing), even when presented with 100% ﬂipped labels. For this reason, we consider all GPT-3 models to be “small” models"
 - where: p.4
3. Semantically-unrelated label ICL (SUL-ICL, Foo/Bar instead of negative/positive) hurts small models far more than large models. Large models lose little, so they learn the input-label mapping.
 - number: none in the main text; the effect is shown only in Fig 3.
 - setup: Fig 3. k=16 per class, 100 eval examples per dataset, averaged over datasets. Defaults: "Input/Output" template and Foo/Bar targets. InstructGPT, Codex, PaLM and GPT-3 were tested. Appendix C.2 says davinci does not follow the trend.
 - quote: "Large models, on the other hand, experience very small performance drops after this change, indicating that they have the ability to learn input–label mappings in-context when the semantic nature of targets is removed."
 - where: p.5, Section 4
4. Instruction tuning does two things at once. It improves learning of input-label mappings, but it strengthens semantic priors more, so tuned models resist flipped labels.
 - number: Flan-PaLM-8B beats PaLM-8B by 9.6% in SUL-ICL. Standard PaLM reaches as low as 31% at 100% flipped. Flan-PaLM does not get below chance.
 - setup: Figs 6 and 7. PaLM vs Flan-PaLM at 8B/62B/540B. Averaged over six datasets, 100 eval examples each. Fig 7 uses k=16 per class. InstructGPT was not compared with GPT-3 because the only difference between those families cannot be isolated.
 - quote: "Flan-PaLM-8B outperforms PaLM-8B by 9.6%, almost catching up to PaLM-62B." and "Flan-PaLM models were unable to override their semantics more than what could be achieved by random guessing, even with 100% ﬂipped labels. Standard PaLM models, on the other hand, could achieve as low as 31% accuracy when presented with 100% ﬂipped labels."
 - where: p.7, Section 5
5. More exemplars help large models more than small ones in SUL-ICL.
 - number: none
 - setup: Fig 4. 2, 4, 8 and 16 exemplars per class. PaLM, Codex and GPT-3 (ada/babbage/curie). InstructGPT and davinci were not run because of cost.
 - quote: "including more in-context exemplars results in a greater performance improvement for large models than it does for small models."
 - where: p.6
6. Some SUL-ICL tasks only work at the largest scale.
 - number: Codex jumps to 80%+ on RTE and ETHOS at code-davinci-002.
 - setup: Fig 5. k=8 per class, 100 eval examples. PaLM is near random on RTE until 540B. PaLM jumps on ETHOS from 8B to 62B. Tasks such as SST-2, TREC, SUBJ and FP are above random even for small models.
 - quote: "the performance on both the RTE and ETHOS datasets is around random for code-cushman-001 and code-davinci-001, then jumps to 80%+ for code-davinci-002."
 - where: p.6
7. SUL-ICL is easier than flipped-label ICL, especially for medium-sized models.
 - number: the gap is up to 74% (text-curie-001 on SST-2).
 - setup: Fig 10, App B.1. k=16 per class, 100 eval examples, per dataset.
 - quote: "medium-sized models perform much worse in the ﬂipped-label setting than they do in the SUL-ICL setting, with performance differing by up to 74% (text-curie-001 on SST-2)."
 - where: p.16
8. Linear classification in context emerges with Codex scale. It is not a clean size effect across families.
 - number: at N=16 the largest Codex beats random by 19%, while smaller ones beat it by at most 9%. code-davinci-002 works up to N=64. Smaller Codex models hit chance near N=16.
 - setup: Fig 8 and Fig 21. Integer coordinates in 1-1000. 100 eval examples, k=16 per class. PaLM scale does not correlate with dimension (all PaLM models work up to at least N=8). Neither family beats a polynomial SVM.
 - quote: "the largest model outperforms random guessing by 19% on this task, while smaller models cannot outperform random guessing by more than 9%."
 - where: p.8; p.26 (C.4)
9. SUL-ICL is robust to the target symbols and to the template, but not to scrambled inputs.
 - number: mean accuracy across input formats is 84.2%, ranging from 77.9% to 87.7%. For targets, no consistent difference was found.
 - setup: App B.3-B.4. code-davinci-002, k=16 per class. Targets: Foo/Bar, 0/1, A/B, Apple/Orange, plus reversed versions. Fig 13 uses 250 eval examples. Fig 14 uses 100 eval examples and six templates. Small models reach chance at 25-50% remapped input words, large models at 75-100%.
 - quote: "the mean accuracy across all NLP tasks for all input formats (which ranges from 77.9% to 87.7%) is within±6.3% of the mean (84.2%)."
 - where: p.19. Remapping is on p.17: "At 100% remapped input words, even the largest models (code-davinci-002 and PaLM-540B) are unable to beat random guessing on almost all datasets."
10. Semantically relevant templates (for example "Review:/Sentiment:") hurt the smallest model. The largest is unaffected.
 - number: none
 - setup: App B.5, Fig 15. Codex family on SST-2, TREC and RTE, using templates from Zhao et al. (2021), k=16 per class.
 - quote: "the smallest Codex model (code-cushman-001) sees performance drop across all tested datasets when switching to semantically-relevant prompt templates. The largest Codex model (code-davinci-002), on the other hand, is relatively unaffected"
 - where: p.20
11. Out-of-distribution robustness in SUL-ICL emerges with scale.
 - number: SST-2 baseline accuracy is 80/91/94/93 for a-1/b-1/c-1/d-1. With SST-2 as exemplars and RT (Rotten Tomatoes) as eval, it is 54/63/90/93. With RT exemplars and SST-2 eval, it is 44/61/90/92.
 - setup: Table 2, InstructGPT ada to davinci-001, 100 eval examples, k=16 per class.
 - quote: "Large models (e.g., text-curie-001 and text-davinci-001), on the other hand, do not suffer from these drops, with text-curie-001 only seeing a 4% decrease in accuracy and text-davinci-001 seeing no significant change in accuracy."
 - where: p.20-21
12. Per-dataset instruction-tuning effects are mixed.
 - number: on SST-2, Flan-PaLM-8B beats PaLM-8B by 28%. On SUBJ, PaLM-8B beats Flan-PaLM-8B by 23%.
 - quote: "PaLM-8B outperforms Flan-PaLM-8B on SUBJ by 23%"
 - where: p.23, C.3

LIMITS
- Each dataset has only 100 randomly sampled eval examples, which the authors chose "to reduce inference costs". Results are averages over datasets, with no confidence intervals. The authors say their questions "depend more on general behaviors than on small performance deltas".
- The tasks are small-label classification: SST-2, SUBJ, TREC, QQP, RTE, FP, ETHOS. There is no generation or reasoning. QNLI and WSC were dropped because even the largest models were near chance.
- Models are 2020-2022 era: GPT-3, InstructGPT, Codex, PaLM and Flan-PaLM. No RLHF chat models or current frontier models were tested. The InstructGPT and Codex sizes are not public and were assumed to increase in order.
- The default is 16 exemplars per class (32 for binary). Fewer exemplars (2-8) appear in Fig 4 and Fig 5 only.
- The mechanism behind the emergence is left open ("an open question that we leave for future work"). In the linear classification task, model size alone did not predict ability (PaLM-540B was no better than PaLM-8B).
- RTE is excluded for PaLM in the flipped and SUL-ICL runs because 16 exemplars per class exceeded the context length.
- Flipped-label accuracy is not exactly 100% minus normal accuracy, because small models sometimes output text that is not one of the labels (footnote 5).
- The authors do not contest Min et al. (2022b). They say their results are "consistent with Min et al. (2022b) for models scaling up to davinci", and that learning input-label mappings appears only in larger models such as PaLM-540B, text-davinci-002 and code-davinci-002.
- Only the abstract and Section 3 say the instruction-tuned flip result holds for "all datasets and model sizes". That is the Fig 20 caption.

BUILDS ON: Brown et al., 2020 (few-shot ICL). Min et al., 2022b (random labels barely matter; the main foil). Min et al., 2022a, Wei et al., 2022a and Chung et al., 2022 (instruction tuning, Flan-PaLM). Wei et al., 2022b (emergence). Rong (2021), which replaced labels with non-alphanumeric characters. Xie et al., 2022 (ICL as latent concept inference). Zhao et al., 2021 (templates). Akyürek et al., 2023, von Oswald et al., 2022 and Garg et al., 2022 (transformers learning linear models in context). Webson & Pavlick, 2022. Tran et al., 2022 (OOD robustness). Chowdhery et al., 2022 (PaLM). Ouyang et al., 2022 (InstructGPT). Chen et al., 2021 (Codex).

CODE: Algorithm 1 gives the linear-classification dataset generation procedure in the appendix. It was not reproduced here; the code is not load-bearing for the note.

FIGURES (captions per figures.py)
- Fig 1, p.2: regular ICL vs flipped-label ICL vs SUL-ICL on a sentiment example. This is the quickest way to explain the three setups.
- Fig 2, p.4: accuracy vs % flipped labels for four model families. The curve for large models falls below the 50% baseline, which shows the emergence.
- Fig 3, p.5: accuracy drop from natural-language targets to Foo/Bar, by model size.
- Fig 6 and Fig 7, p.7: Flan-PaLM vs PaLM on SUL-ICL (better) and on flipped labels (worse).
- Fig 10, p.16: SUL-ICL vs flipped-label performance.
- Fig 12, p.17: remapped-input failure.
- Fig 13, p.18: target types.
- Fig 21, p.26: linear classification by dimension, with an SVM baseline.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Appendix D prompt dumps include offensive hate-speech examples (ETHOS), which are dataset content only. I did not read the per-dataset results in Figures 16-21, which are plots only. Figure axes and legends extract as noise; only caption text and body prose were used for numbers.

Note for the target note: the "Foo/Bar works" claim holds for large models and these classification tasks only. The 90.3 -> 22.5 numbers are an average over six binary tasks for text-davinci-002 at k=16 per class (32 exemplars total). They should not be quoted as a general property of few-shot prompting.
